subject: Cooking
title: Denaturation: What Heat Does to Eggs
description: Learn Denaturation: What Heat Does to Eggs in one minute.

hook.text: A raw egg is translucent and runny. Add heat, and it turns white and firm. What happened?

buildup.text: Egg white is 90% water and 10% protein. Those proteins are tightly folded into coiled shapes.

discovery.text: Heat makes proteins unfold — denature — and bond with neighbors, forming a solid network.

twist.text: This process is irreversible. You can't uncook an egg because the new bonds are permanent.

climax.text: Overcook it and proteins squeeze out water, turning rubbery. Gentle heat keeps eggs tender.

punchline.text: Cooking an egg is a one-way chemistry experiment.

details.summary: Heat causes egg proteins to unfold and bond with each other in a process called denaturation. The white sets at 180°F and the yolk at 158°F. Careful temperature control determines whether eggs become silky custard or rubbery overcooked discs.
details.whyItMatters: Egg denaturation demonstrates how precise temperature control transforms texture. This principle applies to all protein cooking from fish to meat to dairy custards.
takeaways: Egg white proteins set at higher temperatures than yolk proteins
Gentle heat produces soft, creamy textures in custards
Overcooking squeezes out moisture, creating rubbery texture

faq.question: Why do overcooked eggs turn rubbery?
faq.answer: Excessive heat causes proteins to bond too tightly, squeezing out water trapped between them. The result is a dense, dry, rubbery texture. Gentle heat allows proteins to set loosely with water retained between them, creating tenderness.

faq.question: What causes the green ring around hard-boiled yolks?
faq.answer: Iron in the yolk reacts with hydrogen sulfide from the white at high temperatures, forming green ferrous sulfide on the surface. It is harmless but indicates overcooking. Starting eggs in cold water and cooling them immediately prevents the reaction.
